title: New York Below the Waterline: A Survey of the Drowned Districts
body:
# New York Below the Waterline: A Survey of the Drowned Districts

> *Lo! Death has reared himself a throne*
> *In a strange city lying alone*
> *Far down within the dim West*
>
> — Edgar Allan Poe, "The City in the Sea" (1845)

## What Went Under

The inundation of lower Manhattan was not a single event. It was a ratchet — each storm season advancing the waterline another block, each year's high-water mark becoming the next year's baseline, the definition of what was manageable shifting incrementally until the question of management had quietly become irrational.

The last functioning subway station in lower Manhattan — Fulton Street, on what had been the A/C and 2/3 lines — was decommissioned in 2114, when the pump failure rate during routine tidal cycles exceeded the infrastructure authority's maintenance capacity. The trains had stopped running three years earlier. The station stayed open as a transit hub for surface connections until the flooding reached the mezzanine level and the structural inspectors declined to re-certify the stairs. No one announced it was over. The gates were locked. The keys were misfiled. The water continued.

By 2130, the Financial District was navigable by flat-bottomed boat at mean high tide. By 2150, the Battery was fully submerged at all tidal states. By 2180 — when the GLMZ Governance Consortium was assembling its formal zone structure and the corponation era was already thirty years established — the waterline in lower Manhattan ran approximately along the 34th Street corridor. Everything below that line was either underwater or in active contest with the water.

## The Districts Below

The drowned districts of lower Manhattan are not uniform. The depth varies by elevation — the original topography of the island, which was graded and infilled over two centuries of development, reasserts itself as the water returns. The old hills of Manhattan are the least submerged; the old valleys and filled inlets are the deepest.

**The Financial District** — the blocks surrounding the former New York Stock Exchange, the Federal Reserve Bank, Trinity Church — sits at an average of 3.2 meters below mean high tide. On calm days with good visibility, the upper floors of the shorter buildings are visible from the surface: window frames, the tops of ornamental arches, the occasional flag bracket, still holding a bracket where nothing has flown for a century. The NYSE building's facade — the Corinthian columns, the carved *Integrity Protecting the Works of Man* pediment — is a particular destination. At low tide, the pediment clears the water entirely. Guides know the tidal schedule. The tour is not officially sanctioned by anything, because there is no authority left to sanction it.

**Brooklyn's waterfront neighborhoods** — Red Hook, DUMBO, the lower portions of Cobble Hill — are the most visited submerged districts because they are the most accessible. The upper floors of the Red Hook warehouses remain above water and have been occupied continuously since the original evacuation — occupied loosely, by populations that vary with the season and the economy of not having anywhere else. The warehouses are enormous: a single block-long structure can shelter several hundred people in the upper floors while its ground level remains two meters under at high tide. The inhabitants are called, by those who know of them and by themselves, the Upper Floors.

**Lower Manhattan's infrastructure layer** — the former utility tunnels, the subway system, the foundations of the buildings — constitutes the most extensive submerged human-built environment on the East Coast. Bathysphere Networks has surveyed sections of it in connection with potential data infrastructure routing. Their surveys note that the tunnels are remarkably intact: built to last, built deep, built by an era that believed in permanence. The subway tunnels carry no trains and no people. They carry fish. The particular ecosystem that has developed in the drowned Manhattan infrastructure is the subject of ongoing academic interest and no corponation investment.

## The Living City Above

The inhabited New York of the present occupies the high ground: the ridgeline of upper Manhattan from roughly the Harlem River north, the elevated portions of Brooklyn and Queens above the flood zone, the Bronx above the tidal reach of the Harlem and East Rivers. These communities are, in aggregate, a city of perhaps 800,000 people. They are not the New York that the world remembers. They are the New York that outlasted what the world remembered.

The governance of remaining New York is informal in the way that the governance of all post-relevant cities is informal: block associations, neighborhood compacts, whatever agreements could be sustained without the infrastructure of a functioning municipal government. The last elected mayor of New York served her term, and the term after that because there was no mechanism left to hold an election, and then passed administrative responsibility to a council of neighborhood representatives that has no official name and issues no official documents and has administered the inhabited portions of the city for forty years by the simple mechanism of being the only institution present.

The economy is subsistence and service. Food comes from the community gardens that have converted every available surface on the high ground — rooftops, former parks, median strips, the decks of parking structures — to growing space. What cannot be grown is purchased from the inland supply networks that have emerged to serve the post-coastal communities. The trade is in labor and in salvage: the drowned city is full of metal, of glass, of materials that can be recovered by divers and sold to the networks that supply the GLMZ.

Some of the divers are specialists. Some of them are third-generation, trained by parents who were trained by parents who were among the first to understand that the drowned city was an inventory. They know the Financial District's submerged streets the way a librarian knows a collection: this block for copper fittings, that building for structural steel, the former Federal Reserve vault for — nothing, the vault is four meters below high tide and sealed by mechanisms that were designed to be inoperable by anyone without the combination, and the combination was in an office that is now twelve feet underwater. There is a persistent rumor about the gold. There has always been a persistent rumor about the gold.

## The Towers That Remain

Several of the former Manhattan skyscrapers still stand above the waterline. The geography of their survival is the geography of their original height: the taller a building was, the more of it remains visible. The former One World Trade Center site — rebuilt after 2001, built again to 541 meters — stands above the water by more than 400 meters, most of it intact, its lower floors submerged, its upper floors inhabited by no one permanent and visited by people who climb it for reasons ranging from structural salvage to the specific, unclassifiable experience of standing at the top of the tallest building in a drowned city and looking down at what the water has made of everything that was below.

From that height, on a clear day, you can see the waterline running through the city like a geological strata line: the horizontal boundary between what was and what is. Below it, the tops of buildings and the geometry of streets, preserved, undisturbed, the city as it was, minus the people. Above it, the inhabited ridgelines, the gardens, the community structures, the life that reorganized itself on the high ground.

The view is not sad, exactly. It is specific. It is the view of a city that has not ended but has become something the word *city* was not designed to contain.

The water does not have an opinion about this. The water is doing what water does: finding the lowest point, filling it, and continuing.
